summary: Allows transaction-level authentication of DNS messages using shared secrets and one-way hashing. It can authenticate dynamic updates as coming from an approved client, or responses as coming from an approved name server. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 8945.

plainLanguage.summary: TSIG lets two DNS participants use a shared secret to check messages between them. The recipient checks a keyed digest and timing data before accepting a signed message.

questions: how does tsig authenticate dns messages
what is the tsig fudge value
subtitle: How DNS peers use a shared secret to authenticate individual messages.

tldr.problem: DNS clients and servers need an efficient way to check that a transaction came from a party that shares a secret and was not changed in transit.
tldr.mechanism: TSIG adds a record to a DNS message. Its keyed digest covers the message and timing information, and the receiver checks the key, time and digest.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2845 has been obsoleted by RFC 8945. It does not specify how the shared secret is distributed.

today: RFC 2845 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8945. It was updated by RFC 3645, RFC 4635 and RFC 6895.

sections.title: Why DNS Uses a Shared Secret
sections.content:
The RFC presents TSIG as a point-to-point alternative to public-key transaction signatures, which it describes as computationally expensive and complex for simple resolvers. It can authenticate dynamic update requests, responses from a recursive name server and zone transfers.

The two participants must share a secret key. The RFC says this approach is not suitable for general authentication between servers that communicate with many peers, because managing all the shared keys becomes unwieldy.
sections.plainLanguage: TSIG checks messages between two parties that already share a secret. This avoids the public-key work that the RFC says is impractical for some simple DNS clients.

sections.title: The TSIG Record
sections.content:
TSIG is a DNS meta-record with type code 250. It is calculated for a particular transaction and must not be cached. Its fields identify the key and algorithm, give the signing time and allowed time difference, carry the message authentication code, and include an error value.

This RFC specifies HMAC-MD5 as the algorithm that implementations must support. The TSIG record is discarded after it has been used to authenticate the DNS message.
sections.plainLanguage: The TSIG record carries a keyed digest and information needed to check its key and signing time. It is for one transaction and is not kept in a DNS cache.

sections.title: Signing and Checking a Transaction
sections.content:
The sender computes a keyed digest over the DNS message before adding the TSIG record, then appends TSIG to the additional section. A response to a signed request includes a digest that also covers the request's digest, linking the response to that request.

The receiver checks the key, the time values and the digest, in that order. For a TCP exchange containing many DNS messages, TSIG must appear on the first and last messages and at least every hundredth message.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender adds a digest made from the message and shared secret. The receiver checks the key, time and digest, and a signed reply is tied to the signed request.

sections.title: Errors, Clocks and Key Handling
sections.content:
The RFC defines TSIG errors for a bad digest, an unknown key and a time outside the permitted range. A BADTIME response includes the server's current time. The recommended fudge value is 300 seconds, balancing clock differences against the risk of replaying an old message.

The RFC leaves secret distribution outside its scope and expects administrators to configure the communicating systems. It says to protect the keys, use strong random secrets, change them periodically and never send them in cleartext. TSIG authenticates transmission between key holders; it does not prove that the DNS source data is true.
sections.plainLanguage: A failed check can mean the key is unknown, the time is outside the allowed range or the digest is wrong. TSIG checks who sent the message, not whether the information inside it is true.
